cells.tense: The looking is here and the hands are steady enough to work it.
cells.ask: Take the one thing you already do well and run it again tomorrow, slower, on purpose. Notice what you stop needing to check.
cells.core:
You've put in the hours and something has gone quiet in you because of it. The repetition didn't make you sharp — it made you clear. You can look at the thing in front of you and take it in before you decide what it means, and that's not a mood. It's what the practice built.

It shows up as steadiness. Someone hands you something half-finished, or asks a question you don't have ready, and you don't flinch into noise. Not because you're calm by temperament, but because you've seen enough versions to trust your own eye. The light you keep lit is small, and it's enough to work by. What it's free to feed next is whatever you point it at — nothing needs proving.
cells.sheetLine: The practice made you clear, and the clarity is yours to use.
cells.verb: seeing what's actually there before it gets a name
cells.place: the quiet room where one small thing gets run again and again

cells.tense: You are practicing for a version of yourself that hasn't arrived yet.
cells.ask: Pick the smallest piece of the work and do it badly on purpose today. Then stop, and let it sit unfinished.
cells.core:
You're refining ahead of yourself. The drill you're running now is for the moment you imagine is coming — the one where you finally take it in whole, where the eye is trained enough. So every repetition gets measured against a standard that keeps moving, and the work doesn't land. It can't. You're not practicing anymore. You're rehearsing a proof.

More polish won't do it. Taking in what's here is what does it, and here doesn't hold your interest right now because here isn't finished. You've turned the small light into a spotlight on a stage you haven't walked onto. The way out runs through the reverse of what you're doing: fresh eyes, no standard, nothing to demonstrate. Hand yourself the beginner's seat once.

cells.tense: You set the practice down and are still carrying the name of it.
cells.ask: Set a timer for ten minutes and do the thing once, with no plan for the next session. Ten minutes only, then walk away.
cells.core:
There's a door behind you that you used to walk through — the quiet hour, the one small thing done again. You call yourself someone who practices, and the sitting isn't happening. The ability to look didn't leave. The conditions for it did.

Nothing is wrong with your eye. What's empty is the smaller thing: the ordinary, unglamorous repetition that used to feed it. And you won't think your way back into it. The way back runs through a different door than the one you're facing — not trying to look better, but picking one direction and moving deliberately in it. Choosing from what you can see is the muscle. It has gone slack.
cells.sheetLine: The practice stopped and the clear looking went quiet with it.

cells.tense: You keep calling this the situation, not something you are doing.
cells.ask: Write down one thing you noticed this week that someone else missed, and put your name at the top of the page.
cells.core:
You take in what's there before it's named. It happens in ordinary moments — you catch the thing under the thing, the shift in a room, the version of a story that doesn't hold. And then you hand the credit to the situation. You say the work showed it, or anyone would have spotted it, or that's just what happened.

But that noticing is yours. Looking again and again is what built the eye you're looking through, and you talk about it like it belongs to the room. The clear look is already running in you. What hasn't happened is the small plain act of registering that you're the one doing it. That registering costs nothing and changes how you stand in your own work.
cells.sheetLine: You're seeing clearly. You keep calling it the situation.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that this person's steady practice has already produced a first cut of seeing — the record licenses the capacity, not the outcome, and a reader could reasonably say the practice is still mechanical and nothing has opened. The ask survives being wrong because running one repetition slower and staying with it is useful whether or not clarity has arrived, and it teaches the person something about how they hold their own attention either way. The sentence that serves me more than them is any version of 'you already see' in the Unacknowledged cell — it flatters the reading instead of handing them the act of noticing.
